L’origine et la fonction de ce lexique « mazdéanisant » demanderaient toute une étude; peut-être sommes-nous là-même au cœur des problèmes que nous pose le destin religieux de l’Iran. Dans le passé, plusieurs auteurs iraniens y ont été attentifs : Shaykh Azerî Tûsî, Moh. Dârâbî, Rezâ Qolî Khân (Hedâyat), cf. Mo’în, op. cit., pp. 53 ss., et notre introduction, pp. 32 ss. Le fait que le lexique ’irfânî désigne l’Imâm comme Pîr-e Moghân, le grand-maître des Mages, parachève la vision du monde que nous propose l’œuvre de Sohrawardî. Moh. Dârâbî, commentateur du lexique mystique de Hâfez de Shîrâz et de son poème sur le Graal, définit celui-ci comme « une saveur intime (dhawq) qui irradie les lumières des Réalités célestes sur le cœur du mystique ». Nous avons vu que le récit de Sohrawardî se référait à la fois au Graal de Kay Khosraw et au Graal de Jamshîd (Jam). Que l’origine en soit rapportée à l’un ou à l’autre, de toute façon on l’appelle tantôt « Graal montrant le monde », tantôt « Graal voyant le monde », double aspect du motif du microcosme et de l’Homme Parfait. Au cours de son long poème, Mahmûd Shabestarî demande : « Quand donc le Sage t’a-t-il fait le don de ce Graal voyant-le-monde ? » Réponse : « Le jour même où il créait la coupole émaillée du ciel. » Sanâ’î (xiiie s.) emploie le mot pour désigner le cœur. L’embrasement du Graal est alors ici l’illumination du cœur. Après Sohrawardî, Mahmûd Shabestarî a répété, lui aussi, que, si « beaucoup ont disserté sur le Graal », « seule y est initiée l’âme en qui est né l’Homme Parfait... Tout en étant homme, le gnostique (haqîqat-dân) initié à la connaissance de soi-même, est lui-même le Graal de Jamshîd. » Citons encore d’autres poèmes persans du Graal : Awhadî de Marâgha acheva de composer en 733/1332-1333 un poème d’environ cinq mille distiques sur « le Graal de Jamshîd » (Jâm-e Jam), qu’il dédie au lecteur « afin que si tu désires contempler l’univers, tu puisses dans ce Graal contempler ce que tu désires » (tu connaîtras par ce Graal où est le Roi, quelle est sa Demeure, quelle est la Voie). Déjà Awhadî de Kermân (viie/xiiie s.) avait composé un poème intitulé Mesbâh al-Anvâh (Le Flambeau des esprits) où il commente, à l’exemple de Sanâ’î, son ascension spirituelle dans les huit « cités » ou « ciels » des Âmes. Les zoroastriens sont dans le quatrième ciel, le ciel des amants mystiques (nafs-e ’âshiqa) dont la description réunit mazdéens et soufis comme professant la même religion mystique d’amour. Enfin Hâtef Ispahânî (ob. 1198/1784) compose un tarjî’-band qui est un des chefs-d’œuvre de la littérature persane. Composé à la façon d’un oratorio, il montre en somptueuses résonances que le même appel à l’Unification de l’Unique se fait entendre au chapitre des Mages où circule le Graal mystique, dans la cloche du couvent chrétien, et dans les arcanes de la gnose des ’orafâ. Tout le premier band est rempli du lexique mazdéen traditionnel, mais avec une mise en scène dramatique qui pousse à la limite l’audace de la profession de foi ésotérique. ↩

Cf. ibid. notre introduction, pp. 35-36. Le Kanz al-Asrâr est alternativement intitulé Jannat al-wisâl (Le Paradis de l’union). Nous en avions pris connaissance, il y a une vingtaine d’années, à Téhéran, dans un manuscrit aimablement prêté par le Sayyed Mohammad Meshkât; depuis lors, M. Meshkât en a fait don, avec toute sa collection de manuscrits, à la Bibliothèque centrale de l’Université de Téhéran (cf. maintenant Cat. Dânesh-Pajûh, III, 4, pp. 2181 ss.). L’ensemble de l’œuvre se présente en deux forts volumes in-4° (25 × 17 cm), totalisant 1187 pages, le tout écrit en une écriture très fine, le texte étant disposé sur cinq colonnes par page à raison d’environ soixante lignes par page. L’ensemble de l’œuvre fut achevé en 1260/1844; la copie est datée de 1314/1895-96. Le long texte que nous citons ici, concernant Zoroastre comme prophète de la religion d’amour, se trouve au livre XII, p. 1091 (le leitmotiv et le hadîth sont écrits à l’encre rouge, suivant la règle adoptée par le copiste). Qui fut l’auteur de cette énorme rhapsodie? Il ressort du prologue que ce fut un derviche du nom de « Ma’sûm ’Alî ». Cela ouvre le champ à plusieurs hypothèses sur lesquelles on ne peut se prononcer ici. On trouvera dans le catalogue de M. Dânesh-Pajûh (pp. 2178 ss. en note de la description des deux manuscrits de l’œuvre conservés dans la collection) l’incipit et l’explicit de chacun des douze livres. On pourrait croire qu’il n’y eut, à la même époque, qu’une seule œuvre aussi monumentale à s’intituler Jannat al-wisâl. Or il en existe une autre, attestant l’extraordinaire fécondité du soufisme shî’ite en Iran. Cet autre Jannat al-wisâl est une œuvre qui fut commencée par le grand soufi iranien bien connu, Nûr ’Alî-Shâh (ob. 1212/1797-1798); cf. le manuscrit décrit par M. Dânesh-Pajûh, ibid., pp. 2182 ss. L’œuvre de Nûr ’Alî-Shâh aurait dû comprendre huit livres (symbolisant avec les huit portes du paradis). Malheureusement Nûr ’Alî-Shâh mourut avant d’avoir achevé le livre III. Son successeur Rawnaq ’Alî-Shâh (ob. 1225/1810 ou 1230/1814-1815) acheva le livre III et composa les livres IV et V. À son tour Nezâm ’Alî-Shâh Kermânî (ob. 1242/1826-1827) prit la suite et composa les livres VI et VII (cf. Rayhânat IV, n° 428, p. 247). D’après les incipit et les explicit de chacun des sept livres, donnés dans le catalogue (pp. 2184-2188), on doit conclure qu’il ne peut s’agir que de deux œuvres différentes. Une tâche urgente, aussi bien pour la connaissance du soufisme iranien que pour celle de la littérature persane en général, serait une analyse thématique comparée des deux immenses poèmes. Nous croyons savoir que M. Michel de Miras a entrepris ce lourd travail. ↩

Overview of Books I and II

The Islamic world is not a single, undifferentiated whole. Islam as a religion cannot simply be identified with the political idea of the Arab world. There is an Iranian Islam, just as there is a Turkish, Indian, Indonesian, or Malay Islam, among others.

Readers curious about Iran's archaeology and arts, both before and after the coming of Islam, have a wealth of literature at their disposal. Unfortunately, far fewer books answer the question that confronts anyone who wants to understand the motives of Iranian consciousness—the inner impulses that gave these forms their shape.

From the beginning, the Iranian world has formed a distinctive whole within the wider Islamic community. Its character and calling become clear only when we regard Iran's spiritual universe as a continuous whole, before Islam and after it. Islamic Iran has been, above all, the homeland of some of Islam's greatest philosophers and mystics.

For them, speculative thought can never be separated from what it brings to fruition or from its practical consequences. These consequences concern not merely what we today call the social environment, but the whole, concrete world that a person nourishes out of their own being, a world reaching beyond the bounds of earthly life: their spiritual world.

This conviction has guided the author in building the work presented here in seven books. It is the fruit of more than twenty years of research in Iran itself, conducted both in libraries and in the company of Iranian friends, together with the experience of teaching in Paris and Tehran. The method is essentially phenomenological, though it belongs to no particular school of phenomenology. Its aim is to encounter the religious fact by allowing the religious object to show itself as it shows itself to those to whom it appears.
Hence the importance of the book's subtitle: Spiritual and Philosophical Aspects. The very word aspect implies a spectator.

But here the spectator—the phenomenologist—must become a spiritual guest of those to whom the object appears, and must shoulder its weight alongside them. Historical inquiry must therefore remain within the world of the religious object itself, rather than impose some alien category upon it from outside, whether dialectical or otherwise. Only on this condition can the connections suggested throughout this work be drawn across different times, for what we are encountering are variations of one and the same object.
The first two volumes contain Books I and II of the work.

Book I sets out to reveal some of the essential features of Twelver Shiism, also known as Imamism, a tradition firmly rooted in Iran from its earliest days and its official religion since the sixteenth century. These features are identified and studied through what the author has previously called the “phenomenon of the Revealed Book”: the way revelation presents itself to those whom the Qur’an calls Ahl al-Kitâb, the “People of the Book,” embracing Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. In every branch of the Abrahamic tradition, interpreters of the Bible and the Qur’an have confronted the same questions and tasks.

All have sought to discover the Book's true meaning. On each side, that search—the search for the spiritual meaning concealed beneath the literal wording—has produced similar ways of disclosing the esoteric, or inner, meaning of divine revelation. The “phenomenon of the Book” is the source of hermeneutics: the art of understanding and interpreting meaning. The interpreters who sought the hidden meanings of the Bible and the Qur’an probably still have much to teach today's philosophers, who are themselves so preoccupied with hermeneutics.

The technical name for this inner interpretation of the Qur’an is ta’wîl, meaning to “lead back” a thing to its origin, its archetype. Shia metaphysics is governed by two ideas: that God's essence is unknowable, inaccessible, and beyond all naming; and that God reveals himself through the pleroma, the complete heavenly assembly, of Fourteen beings of light, manifested on earth as the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones”: the Prophet, his daughter Fatima, and the Twelve Imams.

The inner meaning that Shia ta’wîl draws from the literal words of the Qur’an concerns, above all, this assembly of Fourteen. It thereby illustrates the distinctive Shia understanding of prophecy, according to which the future of religion cannot be entirely behind us.

Unlike majority Sunni Islam, in which humanity has nothing further to await after the mission of the final Prophet, Shiism keeps the future open. Even after the coming of the “Seal of the Prophets,” something remains to be awaited: the unveiling of the spiritual meaning of the revelations brought by the great prophets. This was the task of interpretation entrusted to the holy Imams, whose teachings fill many volumes.
Yet this spiritual understanding will become complete only at the end of our age, when the Twelfth Imam—now hidden from sight and the mystical pole of this world—appears again.

Interpretation thus entails a particular experience of time, expressed in the division of sacred history into periods: the age of the prophets' missions is followed by the age of spiritual initiation. Here Shia teachings on prophecy meet the hopes of the movement inspired by Joachim of Fiore in the West, with its proclamation of the coming reign of the Spirit.

Yet this division of time already belongs to metahistory, to a reality beyond ordinary historical succession, because its essential concern with the ultimate end of history breaks through the limits of history itself.

Like the interpretation of scripture, the Shia understanding of the Imams confronted its thinkers with problems comparable to those posed by Christology for Christian thinkers. Yet Shia thinkers consistently tended toward solutions rejected by official Christian Christology. Perhaps it was in this way that Shia spiritual knowledge avoided being secularized into a merely social messianism.

Shia metaphysics and Shia spiritual life are inseparable: each is the very substance of the other. For too long, an understanding of Islam limited almost entirely to the Sunni majority has led people to equate Sufism with the spiritual life of Islam as such. In reality, Shia spirituality reaches beyond Sufism. There certainly are Shia Sufi orders, and the spiritual lineages of most tarîqat—Sufi paths or orders—ultimately lead back to one of the Imams.

But a Shia seeker of inner meaning is already, by that very fact, on the spiritual Path (tarîqat), without needing to join a Sufi order. At the summit of a mystical Sinai, knowing the Imam as one's personal guide leads the seeker toward self-knowledge.

Book II is devoted entirely to another equally fundamental feature of the philosophy and spiritual life of Iranian Islam, one that was closely allied from the outset with the Shiism of many Iranian thinkers. Its defining term is ishrâq: sunrise, the coming of dawn (aurora consurgens), the sun's “east.” Just as the philosophy of Ishrâq, understood as a wisdom of Light, is “Oriental” wisdom, so its philosophers—the ishrâqîyân—are “Oriental” philosophers in the metaphysical sense of Orient: the place where light rises. They are also often called “Platonists,” in contrast to the Peripatetic, or Aristotelian, philosophers of Islam.

At the origin of these “Platonists of Persia” stands the heroic resolve of a brilliant young thinker from northwestern Iran: Shihab al-Din Yahya Suhrawardi, who died in Aleppo, Syria, in 1191, at the age of thirty-six, a martyr to his cause. His writings state his purpose plainly: to revive the wisdom of ancient Persia, its philosophy of Light and Darkness; in a sense, to bring the Hellenized Magi home to Islamic Persia. He sought to do so through the very resources of spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl) that Islamic spirituality had placed in his hands.

Some three centuries before the great Byzantine philosopher Gemistos Plethon, this Iranian thinker's work brought together the names of Plato and Zarathustra, or Zoroaster, as heralds of a single “Oriental” tradition reaching back to Hermes, the father of the sages. Plato's Ideas were interpreted in terms of Zoroastrian angelology. His interpretation of being made room for a third world whose reality philosophies of abstract concepts had been unable to establish.

Between the intelligible world and the world of the senses lies the mundus imaginalis, a world entirely real—not the merely “imaginary” world to which outward-looking philosophies reduce it, but a world requiring its own name: the imaginal. Suhrawardi understood that by establishing the reality of this “third world,” he was also establishing the objective reality of prophetic revelations, mystical visions, and the events of revelation. This insight would remain alive throughout the centuries of Iranian thought.

It is significant that this metaphysics of Light identifies light's primordial Source with what Zoroastrian wisdom calls Xvarnah, the “Light of Glory.” From that Source flow the hierarchies of archangels. Their order combines Zoroastrian angelology with the celestial hierarchies described by the Neoplatonist Proclus. The theme of Xvarnah itself carries seemingly inexhaustible echoes and implications. Earlier research has identified correspondences between its manifestations and those of the Holy Grail in Western traditions.

Indeed, the Grail itself—the mystical cup that mirrors the world—appears in the heroic epic of ancient Iran, and it is present in Suhrawardi's writings. There it symbolizes the passage from heroic epic to mystical epic, a decisive event in Iran's cultural history. That same passage is announced in a series of brief tales of spiritual initiation, nearly all written in Persian. Their rich symbolism allows Suhrawardi to lead the reader toward the goal of the reader's longing even more effectively than his great systematic works. The author pays particular attention to two such spiritual tales: one rooted in Iran's own mystical epic, the other in the wider epic of Gnosis, the quest for spiritual knowledge.
Suhrawardi's “Oriental” tradition has remained alive in Iran to the present day. It also exercised a powerful influence in India at the time of Emperor Akbar's religious reforms.

Together, the first two books thus reveal two essential sides of Islamic spiritual knowledge as shaped by the spirit of Iranian Islam. At a time when recent discoveries have given fresh momentum to the study of Gnosis—both ancient Gnosticism and Jewish mystical knowledge—these investigations are especially timely.

Book III is devoted entirely to Iranian Sufism as it emerges from the writings of a great master, Ruzbihan Baqli Shirazi (1128–1209). He was a contemporary of Suhrawardi, the shaykh al-Ishrâq, or Master of Illumination.
But where Suhrawardi was a man of northern Iran, Ruzbihan belonged to the south: to Fars, the province known in antiquity as Persis, Persia in the strict sense.

His writings and teachings are especially revealing of the spirituality of Iranian Sufism, above all in what distinguishes it from traditional Christian asceticism. The phenomenon of the “unhappy consciousness,” familiar to us from Hegel, belongs specifically to the experience of Christian consciousness—even if today that consciousness increasingly insists on being “present in the world,” ashamed of its unhappiness or hoping thereby to be less unhappy.

Sufism, too, encounters an opposition that must be overcome; but the terms of that opposition differ from those that make, or have made, the Christian's condition so troubled. The Christian has found himself torn between sin and the grace that justifies, belief and knowledge; more crudely, between “mysticism” and “sensuality”; more abstractly, between the truth of historical fact and inward truth, between the object of faith embodied in history and spiritual reality unconditioned by time, between the literal content of revelation and its spiritual meaning, and so forth.

So much so that, as a post-Christian order of things becomes secularized, the illness merely changes its name. Sociology takes theology's place as the ruling authority, with the assistance of psychoanalysis. People speak no longer of sin but of guilt complexes, frustration, and so on.

The Sufi, by contrast, is neither a sinner, nor a patient, nor a frustrated individual. He feels no need to be “justified.” He is a stranger, an exile. Like seekers of spiritual knowledge in every age and place, he longs to find his way home, and therefore to meet the guide who will show him the road back. For him, this is the meaning of prophecy: the religious Law (sharî’at) revealed by the Prophet opens the inner Path (tarîqat) leading to spiritual Truth (haqîqat).
